chapters.title: Chapter 5: Putting Your Tax Plan Into Action

lessons.title: Common 80C Mistakes: The March Rush, Wrong Products and Missed Claims

children.text: Most 80C mistakes are not about getting the law wrong. They happen because of timing, pressure and habit: a deadline in March, a persuasive relationship manager, a policy bought because "everyone does it". This lesson collects the costliest mistakes Indian taxpayers make, shows what each one really costs, and gives you a fix for every one.

body.text: The most expensive 80C mistake is not missing a deduction. It is locking money into the wrong product for years to save tax you might not even owe.

body.title: Two ways to fill the same ₹1,00,000 gap

columns.label: The March rush
points: HR proof deadline email arrives in January
Panic, then a quick call to the bank relationship manager
Buys whatever is offered: often an insurance policy or tax saver FD
₹1,00,000 lump sum enters the market on one day, whatever the level

points: Calculates the real 80C gap in April after counting EPF, fees and insurance

body.title: Spot the Red Flag
body.question: On 28 March, Deepa's bank relationship manager in Hyderabad calls with a 'last-minute tax saving plan'. Which statement in his pitch should worry her most?
options: 'You pay ₹1,00,000 a year for 15 years, and you get guaranteed returns plus life cover.'
'The premium receipt can be submitted to HR as proof.'
body.explanation: A 15-year premium commitment sold as 'guaranteed returns plus life cover' is the classic description of a traditional endowment or money-back plan. These typically return 4% to 6% a year with low cover. The other statements are true of many products and are not warning signs on their own. The real question is whether a 15-year commitment fits her goals, which a March phone call cannot answer.

children.text: Mistake 2: Investing Without Checking Your Regime

body.text: The new regime is the default. If you never chose the old regime, and it would not actually be cheaper for you, every rupee you put into 80C products saves you nothing in tax. Before buying anything for tax, compare your tax under both regimes. For many salaried taxpayers earning up to about ₹12.75 lakh, the new regime already brings tax to zero.

children.text: Mistake 3: Filling a Bucket That Is Already Full

body.title: Your Turn: The Overflow
body.prompt: Suman, a lecturer in Patna on the old regime, has employee EPF of ₹90,000 and pays ₹70,000 in tuition fees for her two children. In March, she buys a ₹50,000-a-year endowment policy 'for 80C'. By how much do her eligible payments now exceed the ₹1,50,000 limit?
body.explanation: EPF ₹90,000 + tuition ₹70,000 = ₹1,60,000, already ₹10,000 over the limit before the policy. Adding ₹50,000 takes her to ₹2,10,000, which is ₹60,000 over. The endowment policy adds zero to her deduction and commits her to years of premiums.

body.title: Frequently Missed Deductions: Flip to See Why

cards.definition: Paid when you buy a house, they qualify under Section 123 (80C) in the year of payment. Many first-time buyers never claim them.
Only interest is widely known. The principal part of your EMI also qualifies under 80C. Check your lender's certificate.
Interest accrued in years 1 to 4 counts as a fresh 80C investment each year. Most NSC holders never claim it.
Premiums for life cover on your spouse or children qualify, not just your own policy.
A separate Section 126 (80D) limit of up to ₹50,000 for senior citizen parents, over and above your own family.
Section 124(3) sits outside the ₹1.5 lakh limit. Once 80C is full, it is the next deduction to use.
Up to ₹10,000 under Section 153 (80TTA). Easy to forget because it is small and automatic.

body.title: Your Turn: The Forgotten NSC Interest
body.prompt: Farhan, a pharmacist in Lucknow on the old regime, is in the 30% slab and has room left in his 80C limit. His NSC accrued ₹12,439 of interest in its second year, which he reported as income but did not claim under 80C. How much tax did he miss saving, including 4% cess? Round to the nearest rupee.
body.explanation: ₹12,439 × 30% × 1.04 = ₹3,881. He paid tax on the interest as income but skipped the matching deduction, so he was taxed on it without the offsetting benefit.

children.text: Mistake 5: Assuming You Can Fix It Later

body.title: Fixing a return: revised vs updated

columns.label: Revised return
points: Corrects any mistake in a return already filed, including missed deductions
Can increase your refund
Section 263(5): up to 12 months from the end of the tax year (31 March 2028 for tax year 2026-27), with a fee if filed after 9 months
This is the right tool for a forgotten 80C claim

columns.label: Updated return
points: Section 263(6) of the Income-tax Act, 2025 (139(8A) under the 1961 Act)
Available for up to 48 months, with additional tax of 25% to 70% depending on delay
Can only add income or increase tax
Cannot be used to claim a missed deduction or a refund

body.title: Quick Check
body.textWithBlank: An updated return can only ___ your tax liability, so it cannot be used to claim a forgotten 80C deduction.
body.explanation: Updated returns exist to let taxpayers disclose missed income voluntarily. For a missed deduction, use a revised return before its deadline.

body.title: Go Deeper: Clawback Traps That Reverse Past Deductions

content.caption: When 80C deductions already claimed get added back to your income

Sold within 5 years from the end of the tax year in which you got possession
Stopping a traditional life policy
Premiums stopped within 2 years
Surrendering a ULIP
Within 5 years
Closing SCSS early
Deductions reversed along with a 1% or 1.5% penalty
Withdrawing EPF early
Before 5 years of continuous service

body.title: Scenario: Audit Varun's Plan
body.scenario: Varun, 30, is a developer in Kolkata earning ₹14,00,000. He never told HR his regime choice. His employee EPF is ₹57,600. In March, he buys a traditional policy with a ₹1,00,000 yearly premium and a ₹8,00,000 sum assured from his bank, plus a ₹50,000 tax saver FD, all 'to save tax'. He plans to file his return in September because July is busy at work.
body.prompt: List every mistake in Varun's plan. Then compare his tax under both regimes, assuming only the standard deduction and 80C. Was any of it worth it?
body.modelAnswer: Mistakes: he never checked his regime; his EPF, policy and FD total ₹2,07,600, far above ₹1,50,000; the policy premium is 12.5% of the sum assured, so only ₹80,000 is deductible and the maturity will be taxable; the FD locks money for 5 years; and filing in September means a belated return, which forces the new regime. Now the numbers. Old regime: ₹14,00,000 minus ₹50,000 standard deduction minus ₹1,50,000 under 80C gives taxable income of ₹12,00,000. Tax is ₹12,500 + ₹1,00,000 + ₹60,000 = ₹1,72,500, plus 4% cess = ₹1,79,400. New regime: ₹14,00,000 minus ₹75,000 gives ₹13,25,000. Tax is ₹20,000 (4 to 8 lakh at 5%) + ₹40,000 (8 to 12 lakh at 10%) + ₹18,750 (12 to 13.25 lakh at 15%) = ₹78,750, plus cess = ₹81,900. The new regime is about ₹97,500 cheaper even with a full 80C claim on the old regime, so none of his March purchases saved any tax. He should keep the policy only if it genuinely suits him after checking surrender and paid-up values, consider a term plan for real cover, choose future investments on merit, and file by 31 July.

body.title: An 80C Calendar That Prevents Every Mistake
steps: April: compare both regimes and declare your choice to HR
April: add up EPF, tuition fees, insurance and home loan principal to find your real gap
April: set up SIPs or standing instructions for the gap, with PPF deposits before the 5th
Any time a policy is pitched: check premium vs 10% of sum assured, lock-in and actual return
December: confirm investments match your declaration
January to February: submit proofs, including stamp duty, NSC interest and spouse's policies
June to July: check Form 130, Form 168 and AIS, then file by 31 July
After filing: if you spot a missed deduction, file a revised return before its deadline

points: Check your regime before investing; on the new regime, 80C products save nothing.
Count EPF, tuition fees, insurance and home loan principal before buying anything new.
Plan in April and invest monthly instead of rushing into products in March.
Commonly missed claims include stamp duty, home loan principal, NSC reinvested interest and spouse's policies.
A forgotten deduction can be fixed with a revised return, not an updated return.
Watch the clawback traps: early house sale, early policy exit and early EPF withdrawal.

body.text: This lesson is for educational purposes only and is not tax, legal or investment advice. Return deadlines, slab rates and clawback rules can change with each Union Budget. Consult a qualified Chartered Accountant for decisions specific to your situation.
